Buying an unbiased copy of a bit costs $1$, so the noisy model is at least as powerful as the query model.

Buying a copy of $x_i$ at bias $\gamma = 1$ costs $\gamma^2 = 1$ and returns the bit exactly, so the noisy model contains the query model verbatim and the budget $\sum_i \gamma_i^2$ counts queries. The simulation is output-blind, so it holds for search problems -- which matters, because it is the only direction that survives there.

partial:
partial Settled #

Upper bounds — holds for every partial

  • \(\mathrm{noisyR}(f) \le \mathrm{R}(f)\)
    BenDavidBlais20composition
    Buying an unbiased copy of a bit costs $1$, so the noisy model is at least as powerful as the query model.
  • \(\mathrm{noisyR}(f) = \Theta\big(\mathrm{R}(f\circ \mathrm{GapMaj}_n)\,/\,\mathrm{R}(\mathrm{GapMaj}_n)\big)\)
    BenDavidBlais20composition
    Theorem 4: an exact characterisation, not just a bound, with $n$ the input size of $f$ and $\mathrm{R}(\mathrm{GapMaj}_n)=\Theta(n)$. It holds for relations too, provided two inputs have disjoint allowed output sets; and combined with Theorem 3 it gives Corollary 5, $\mathrm{R}(f\circ g) = \Omega\big(\tfrac{\mathrm{R}(f\circ\mathrm{GapMaj}_n)}{\mathrm{R}(\mathrm{GapMaj}_n)}\mathrm{R}(g)\big)$ -- a composition theorem with no complexity measure in it at all. The easy direction is Theorem 3; the hard direction needs the normal form of Theorem 39, that an optimal noisy algorithm can be taken to use only biases $1$ and $1/\sqrt n$, which are simulated by reading a whole $\mathrm{GapMaj}_n$ gadget and by reading one random bit of it respectively.

Lower bounds / separations — there is a family achieving this

  • \(\mathrm{R}(f)=\Theta(n)\ \Rightarrow\ \mathrm{noisyR}(f)=\Theta(\mathrm{R}(f))\)
    CKMPSS23

Noisy complexity is the optimal outer measure in randomized composition [BenDavidBlais20composition]. For partial Boolean f on n bits, it is now at least $\Omega(\mathrm{R}(f)/\log(n+1))$ [PednekarPodder26STOC]. Constant-factor equality is false even for total functions [Meiburg26composition], as \(W_q\) shows. The non-adaptive pair remains equivalent within constants.

see also: \(\mathrm{noisyR}(f)\), \(\mathrm{R}_{\varepsilon}(f)\), \(\mathrm{N}_{p}(f)\), \(\mathrm{GapMaj}^{\delta}_{n}\), Two different noisy query models, \(\mathrm{ApproxIndex}_k\) data/relations/04-composition.yaml
relation:
relation Settled #

Upper bounds — holds for every relation

  • \(\mathrm{noisyR}(f) \le \mathrm{R}(f)\)
    BenDavidBlais20composition
    Buying a copy of $x_i$ at bias $\gamma = 1$ costs $\gamma^2 = 1$ and returns the bit exactly, so the noisy model contains the query model verbatim and the budget $\sum_i \gamma_i^2$ counts queries. The simulation is output-blind, so it holds for search problems -- which matters, because it is the only direction that survives there.

Recorded at the relational level because the reverse direction is exactly where relations break: $\mathrm{R}$ is unbounded in terms of $\mathrm{noisyR}$ on \(\mathrm{AGREE}_n\), the relational barrier of [BenDavidBlais20composition]. The partial-function record carries the interesting content (Theorem 4, the $\mathrm{GapMaj}$ characterisation).

see also: \(\mathrm{noisyR}(f)\), \(\mathrm{R}_{\varepsilon}(f)\), \(\mathrm{noisyR}^{\mathrm{na}}(f)\), \(\mathrm{AGREE}_n\), Is …? data/relations/13-definitional.yaml

facts: $\mathrm{noisyR}(f) \le \mathrm{R}(f)$ always, and the two are not within a constant: $\mathrm{R}$ can be exponentially larger for partial $f$ (\(\mathrm{ApproxIndex}_k\)). Whether $\mathrm{R} = 2^{O(\mathrm{noisyR})}$ in general is open.
$\mathrm{R}(f\circ g^n) = \Omega(\mathrm{noisyR}(f)\,\mathrm{R}(g))$, and $\mathrm{noisyR}$ is the largest measure with this property [BenDavidBlais20composition].

Lemma 37 of [BenDavidBlais20composition]: $\mathrm{noisyR}(f) = \Omega(1)$ for every non-constant $f$, and more precisely distinguishing two inputs that differ on a block $B$ costs $\Omega(1)$ inside $B$. Both hold for relations with two inputs whose allowed output sets are disjoint.

Lemma 38: $\mathrm{noisyR}(f) = \Omega(\mathrm{fbs}(f))$, by LP-weighting the previous item over the sensitive blocks. Composed with $\mathrm{R} = O(\mathrm{fbs}^3)$ this gives a complexity-only bound for total $f$. The new input-size-dependent bound is $\mathrm{R}=O(\mathrm{noisyR}\log(n+1))$ for partial Boolean functions [PednekarPodder26STOC].
Normal form (Lemmas 36, Theorem 39): an optimal noisy algorithm may be assumed to use only two bias values, $\gamma = 1$ and $\gamma = 1/\sqrt n$.

For every nonconstant partial Boolean $f$ on $n$ bits, $\mathrm{R}(f)\le C\log(n+1)\mathrm{noisyR}(f)$ [PednekarPodder26STOC, Theorem 31]. This closes Is …?. Total functions nevertheless have $\mathrm{R}/\mathrm{noisyR}=\Omega((\log N)^{1/4}/\log\log\log N)$ [Meiburg26composition, Theorem 4.1].

self.short: Randomized complexity when the algorithm may buy a biased (noisy) copy of any bit at cost proportional to bias squared.

lo.note:
A single character has sparsity $1$ and $\mathrm{osss} = 1$: the two agree, but neither
grows, so this witnesses no exponent. No function in the zoo has $\mathrm{osss}$ growing
while $\mathrm{spar}$ stays bounded -- indeed $\mathrm{spar}(f) = O(1)$ forces $f$ to be a
constant-size combination of characters, and $\mathrm{osss}$ is then bounded too.
